name: Prussian Red
lede: Prussian red was an old trade name for a brownish iron-oxide red, and it has nothing to do with Prussian blue except the country.

sections.title: A name without a single recipe
sections.body: The Pigment Compendium calls Prussian red a widely used term in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries for a modified earth or a synthetic iron oxide [1]. Watin, in 1785, treats it as either a calcined earth or, more likely, caput mortuum or colcothar, and links it to Nürnberg red [1][2]. As late as 1874, Riffault still gives Nürnberg red as another name for Prussian red [2]. Books disagree on what exactly it was, because the label named a look, not a method [1][2].

sections.title: Where it sits among the iron reds
sections.body:
Salter, in 1869, lists Prussian red among the many synonyms of red ochre, along with English red, Persian red, Spanish brown and others [3]. Colcothar, the iron oxide left after distilling sulfuric acid from iron sulfate, was equated by Watin with caput mortuum and, through it, with Prussian red [4]. For the family, see [[venetian-red]], [[indian-red]], [[english-red]] and [[tuscan-red]].

One trap: the name does not mean a red made from [[prussian-blue]]. That pigment has its own relatives, such as a brown made by roasting it, which the same compendium lists under Prussian brown, a separate entry [5].

sections.title: The swatch
sections.body: The swatch here, #895B51, is a muted, brownish red from Ridgway's 1912 color atlas, later sets echoing it [6]. It is a modern standard color, and the old pigment varied by maker [1][2]. Treat it as one point in a range.

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
Our name graph records Prussian red from Ridgway in 1912, with Maerz and Paul in 1930 and ISCC-NBS in 1955 [6].

In our archive of 23,781 paintings, this color appears in 410 paintings, 1.72 per cent, and by the within-painting measure in 172 [7]. It is more common than 68 per cent of the named colors [7]. It peaks in the 1900s, in 33 of 1,674 paintings, 2.0 per cent, or 2.4 times the expected rate [7]. In 34 per cent of the 172 paintings it plays an accent [7]. These are photographs of aged, varnished paintings, so a match is not a pigment test [7].
